t0_0.what: Definition: Vitest is configured from the vite.config.ts block in test. For component tests, environment: 'jsdom', globals: true (describe/it global), and jest-dom matchers are imported in setupFiles.
t0_0.why: Vite uses the same transform pipeline, so aliases, TS, JSX work without separate configuration. Watch mode provides instant feedback like HMR.
cons: Some Jest-specific plugins/mocks behave differently
gotchas: Add TS types (vitest/globals) when using globals: true
The default environment is node — set jsdom for DOM tests
In CI use vitest run (no watch)
terms: Vite-native test runner — Jest-like API, but very fast and ESM/TS out of the box.
node (default) or jsdom/happy-dom — use jsdom when you need a DOM.
File that runs before each test (extends matchers, starts MSW).

t0_1.what: Definition: describe groups tests, it/test is a case, expect(value).matcher() is an assertion. test.each runs the same logic on multiple data sets.
t0_1.why: Tests also serve as documentation: name them so that when they fail you know what broke. Table-driven tests eliminate duplication.
cons: Over-specified tests break during refactoring.
gotchas: Object comparisons fail with toBe — use toEqual or toStrictEqual.
Check only one behavior per test.
Use snapshots sparingly — large snapshots are not reviewed.
terms: Table-driven tests: one test, many input/output rows.

t0_2.what: Definition: Mocks dependencies (API, timers, modules) to fake them so that tests stay fast and deterministic. Behaviour is set with mockReturnValue, mockResolvedValue, mockImplementation; reset with vi.clearAllMocks()/restoreAllMocks().
t0_2.why: A unit test should not depend on the network or database. However, excessive mocking ties you to the implementation — mock at boundaries (network, time), not on internal functions.
cons: Over-mocking makes tests brittle
gotchas: vi.mock is hoisted to the top of the file — use vi.hoisted for variables defined above
Reset mocks between tests
For network, MSW module-mock is better
terms: Wraps an existing method to track or override it.

t0_3.what: Definition: In async tests, use async/await and always await/return, otherwise the test passes prematurely. For time-based code, use fake timers: advanceTimersByTime(ms).
t0_3.why: Sleeping on real setTimeout makes tests slow and flaky. Fake timers let you test debounce/polling logic in milliseconds.
cons: Interaction between fake timers and promises is tricky (needs async variants)
gotchas: If you forget await, the test passes without any assertion
Restore real timers after fake timers with useRealTimers
Use advanceTimersByTimeAsync with promises
terms: Retry until the condition becomes true (RTL).

t0_4.what:
Definition: vitest run --coverage creates a report (lines, branches, functions). Coverage shows what was executed, not whether it was correctly verified.

Exclude config, types, trivial getters, and generated code; focus on branch coverage for critical logic.
t0_4.why: Aiming for 100% coverage encourages gaming and useless tests. Better: high coverage on critical paths plus a threshold so it doesn’t fall.
cons: Coverage does not guarantee quality
gotchas: Executed ≠ asserted: tests without asserts also contribute to coverage.
Don’t treat coverage as a target; treat it as a signal.
Branch coverage is more useful than line coverage.
terms: v8: native, fast; istanbul: instrumentation, more accurate branches.

t0_5.what: Definition: Lifecycle hooks (beforeAll, beforeEach, afterEach, afterAll) handle setup/teardown. In a nested describe, hooks run according to their scope. test.todo is a marker for planned tests.
t0_5.why: Tests that depend on test order are flaky and difficult to debug. Each test should create its own data and clean it up.
cons: Heavy beforeAll shared state can break isolation
gotchas: it.only should not be committed — the entire suite gets skipped in CI.
Shared module-level variables leak between tests.
Use async/await inside hooks.
terms: Each test runs independently — no shared mutable state.
Temporarily skip, run only this, or mark as pending.

// don't commit with it.only left in — CI lint: no-only-tests

t1_0.desc: "The more your tests resemble the way your software is used, the more confidence they give you." Avoid testing state, class names, internal functions.
t1_0.what: Definition: RTL's motto: 'The more your tests resemble the way your software is used, the more confidence they give you.' Render the component, interact like a user (click, type), and assert what appears on the screen.
t1_0.why: Implementation tests (state variable name, instance method) break on refactor even if the app works fine. Behaviour tests only break when a user-facing thing changes.
cons: Real browser behaviours (layout) are not in jsdom
gotchas: Do not test the component's internal state/hooks
Do not over-depend on snapshots
Layout/CSS checks require E2E/visual tests
terms: Test what the user sees/experiences, not state/internal function.
The more the test resembles real use, the more confidence.
Tests do not break when implementation changes.

t1_1.why: Role-based queries validate accessibility simultaneously: if getByRole('button', {name}) succeeds, a screen-reader user will also receive it.
cons: Learning curve to understand role/name
gotchas: getBy throws an error on multiple matches — use getAllBy
For absence checks, use queryBy instead of getBy
testId only as a last resort
terms: The most preferred query — using accessible role + name.
getBy: immediate or error; queryBy: returns null; findBy: async wait.
Last resort when no semantic query is available.

t1_2.what: Definition: @testing-library/user-event runs the full sequence hover → mousedown → focus → mouseup → click on a click, and on type each key triggers keydown/keyup. fireEvent.click only generates a single click event.
t1_2.why: The test mimics real browser behavior (e.g., clicking a disabled button does nothing). Therefore user-event should be the default.
cons: a bit slower and asynchronous compared to fireEvent
gotchas: In v14, call userEvent.setup() first and await it
Use fireEvent only when user-event does not support it (e.g., some custom events)
Provide the advanceTimers option when using fake timers
terms: Real user interactions simulate the full sequence of focus, pointer, and keyboard events.
Only dispatches a single low-level DOM event.
Create an instance, then await it before use (v14).

t1_3.what: Definition: For async UI (showing data after an API) use await screen.findByText(). waitFor retries the assertion; waitForElementToBeRemoved waits for the loading spinner to disappear.
t1_3.why: Fixed sleeps (setTimeout) are slow and flaky. Polling-based waits run until the condition becomes true and finish quickly.
cons: Timeout default 1 s — increase it for slow cases
gotchas: Do not perform side effects (click) inside waitFor
Keep only one assertion per waitFor
'not wrapped in act' warning is often a signal that await is missing
terms: getBy + waitFor: wait until the element appears.
Retry the callback until it passes or times out.
Allows React to flush state updates; RTL usually wraps it automatically.
codeSwap: // bad: side effects waitFor ke andar
// ❌ will be clicked again and again

t1_4.what: Definition: A component needs context (Router, React Query, Redux), so create a renderWithProviders helper that provides a wrapper. Mock child components only when they are very heavy or third-party (chart, map).
t1_4.why: Repeating providers in every test is noisy. Excessive mocking (of our own child components) pushes tests away from integration and makes them brittle.
cons: Over-mocking reduces confidence
gotchas: Create a new QueryClient for each test (to avoid cache leaks).
Set query retry to false in tests.
Do not mock your own child components.
terms: Render wrapper with providers (Router, QueryClient, Theme).
Mock only network/browser APIs, not your child components.

t1_5.what: Definition: axe(container) runs WCAG rules on the rendered DOM (missing labels, bad contrast, invalid ARIA). Role-based RTL queries are also implicit accessibility tests.
t1_5.why: It is a cheap way to catch regressions. However, keyboard flow and screen-reader experience must be verified manually or via E2E (Playwright + axe).
cons: Color contrast and layout rules do not run in jsdom.
gotchas: Passing axe does not mean fully accessible.
Contrast checks are performed in a real browser (Playwright).
Keyboard navigation tests need to be written separately.
terms: Automation catches only ~30–40% of accessibility issues.

t2_0.what: Definition: MSW intercepts requests at the real network layer, so fetch/axios/React Query code doesn't even know it's a mock. In Node use setupServer(...handlers), in the browser a service worker.
t2_0.why: Module-level mocks (vi.mock('axios')) stick to the code's approach. With MSW the same code runs as in production — only the response is fake.
cons: Initial setup and maintaining handlers
gotchas: onUnhandledRequest: 'error' makes unmocked calls appear immediately
Start the server in a shared setup file
Use msw v2 with global fetch in Node 18+
terms: Mock Service Worker — intercepts requests at the network level.
listen() before all, resetHandlers() after each, close() after all.

t2_1.what: Definition: Handlers are created with http.get/post/put/delete(url, resolver). The resolver can read the request (await request.json(), query params) and returns an HttpResponse.
t2_1.why: If a handler set behaves like a realistic backend (validation, 404), it is useful for both tests and development.
cons: Handlers can drift away from the backend.
gotchas: For relative URLs, the base URL must be set in the environment
The request body can be read only once — clone it
Order matters: the first matching handler wins
terms: A mock of a route: method + path + resolver.
Helper to create a response: HttpResponse.json(data, { status }).

t2_2.what: Definition: Not only the happy path, also test error and loading states: 4xx/5xx responses, network failure, slow response (await delay(500)) and empty list.
t2_2.why: Production bugs often occur in error/empty/loading states that are not manually tested. You can make all of these deterministic with MSW.
cons: Testing many scenarios can make the test suite long.
gotchas: Turn off retries in tests for clients with retry logic (React Query).
delay('infinite') always shows a loading state.
Keep the error format the same as the backend.
terms: Latency simulation: for testing loading states.

t2_3.what: Definition: Default handlers serve the happy path; if a single test needs a different response, override it with server.use(http.get(...)). afterEach(() => server.resetHandlers()) clears the overrides.
t2_3.why: You don’t need a separate handlers file for each scenario. The override applies only to that test, so isolation is maintained.
cons: If you forget resetHandlers, you get leaks
gotchas: Call resetHandlers in afterEach
Overrides match before defaults
Parallel tests share the same server — keep files isolated
terms: Override the handler for a test.
Handler runs only on the first request.
codeSwap: retry scenario: pehli call fail, doosri pass
retry scenario: first call fails, second passes

t2_4.what: Definition: GraphQL posts everything to a single endpoint, so MSW matches by operation name instead of URL: graphql.query('GetUser', ...).
t2_4.why: You can test clients like Apollo, urql, or React Query without changing them. By inspecting variables you can provide conditional responses.
cons: The operation must have a name (anonymous queries do not match)
gotchas: GraphQL errors come with a 200 status, not an HTTP error
Give the query a name (do not keep it anonymous)
Both partial data and errors can be present
terms: You can read variables in the resolver.
Scoped handlers for a specific endpoint URL.

t2_5.what: Definition: Reuse src/mocks/handlers.ts in Vitest (setupServer), browser development (setupWorker) and Playwright (page.route or MSW). Data builders/factories are also shared.
t2_5.why: If the API contract changes, it must be updated in one place. The frontend can be developed without the backend and tests see the same data that appears in development.
cons: Handlers need to stay in sync with the real API (contract tests help)
gotchas: Ensure mock data does not end up in the production bundle (use dynamic import + environment guard)
The service worker file must be in the public folder (msw init)
Catch handler drift with contract tests
terms: A single handlers.ts used by tests, Playwright, and dev mode.
Common mock data in one place.
Start MSW in the browser to develop the UI without a backend.

t3_0.what: Definition: In the Playwright config, projects define separate browsers/devices, use.baseURL, retries (1–2 on CI), workers (parallelism) and reporter (html/github) are set. webServer starts the app automatically.
t3_0.why: Cross-browser coverage (especially WebKit/Safari) is a major benefit of E2E. Trace on first retry makes debugging failures easier.
cons: Browser downloads and CI time
gotchas: On CI you need npx playwright install --with-deps
Retries hide flakiness — fix by examining the trace
Keep data isolated for parallel tests
terms: Configuration for projects (browsers), baseURL, retries, workers, reporters.
Same tests on chromium / firefox / webkit / mobile viewports.
Start the dev/preview server before the test.

t3_1.what: Definition: Create locators from user-facing queries: getByRole, getByLabel, getByText, getByTestId. Chain/filter: page.getByRole('listitem').filter({ hasText: 'Asha' }).
t3_1.why: CSS/XPath selectors break during UI refactors. Role-based locators are stable and also encourage accessibility. Manual waitForTimeout is not needed.
cons: Ambiguous locators cause strict mode errors (good signal)
gotchas: Avoid waitForTimeout — web-first assertions (expect(...).toBeVisible())
CSS class selectors are fragile
Assertions on locator.count() do not retry — use toHaveCount
terms: Playwright automatically checks actionability (visible, enabled, stable) before an action.
If a locator matches multiple elements, it throws an error — catches ambiguity.

t3_2.what: Definition: In POM, a class is created for each page/component that exposes locators and actions (login(email, pw)). Tests are written in business language, not with selectors.
t3_2.why: In large suites, selectors get duplicated; a UI change can break 30 tests. POM makes maintenance cheaper. In small suites it can be overkill.
cons: Extra abstraction; overkill in small projects
gotchas: Keep assertions minimal in page objects (assert in tests)
Avoid very deep inheritance (BasePage chains)
Also create component-level objects (Modal, Table)
terms: Wrapping page interactions in a class.
Selectors and flows in one place — update a single file when UI changes.
Playwright way to inject a page object into a test.

t3_3.what: Definition: In every test, logging in through the UI is slow. A setup project logs in and saves a storageState file; the remaining tests start authenticated using use: { storageState }. Fixtures can be worker-scoped or test-scoped.
t3_3.why: A large part of the E2E suite is spent on authentication and data setup. Fixtures and saved state make tests run faster and isolated.
cons: Be aware when the shared state file expires or rotates.
gotchas: Do not commit the .auth folder to git
Shared mutable data between tests can cause flakiness
Always perform cleanup in the fixture after (await use(x))
terms: Setup for a test that is created and cleaned up automatically (test.extend).
Runs once before the entire run.

t3_4.what: Definition: The first run creates a baseline snapshot; subsequent runs compare against it. Use --update-snapshots for intentional UI changes. Mask dynamic content with mask or disable animations with animations: 'disabled'.
t3_4.why: CSS regressions (spacing, overflow, wrong color) that functional tests miss are caught by visual tests. However, OS/font differences can be noisy — create baselines only in CI (Linux, Docker).
cons: Noisy and requires maintaining baselines
gotchas: Baselines on local macOS and CI Linux will differ
Animations and lazy-loaded images can cause flaky diffs
Don’t screenshot everything — only high-value screens
terms: Compares the page/element pixel-by-pixel with the baseline image.

t3_5.what: Definition: page.route('**/api/items', route => route.fulfill({ json })) is used to mock the network layer. Seed test data from the API with a real backend for E2E (request fixture).
t3_5.why: Third-party, flaky, or rare cases (500 error, slow response) are mocked to make them deterministic; and the core happy path uses a real backend so that the contract is also tested.
cons: Over-mocking reduces the realism of E2E.
gotchas: Register the route before page.goto.
Glob patterns must match precisely.
Too much mocking reduces the benefit of E2E.
terms: Intercepts a network request to fulfill, abort, or modify.
Mock: fake response; seed: create data in the real backend via the API.
Reuse the same handlers in E2E.

t4_0.what: Definition: TDD loop: first a failing test (red), then the simplest code that makes it pass (green), then refactor. Pure logic and bug fixes (first repro test) benefit the most; UI/exploratory work may incur overhead.
t4_0.why: Small steps, fast feedback and testable design are obtained. But turning it into a dogma and applying it to every line can reduce productivity — judgment is needed.
cons: May feel slow in exploratory / UI-heavy work
gotchas: If you write tests around the implementation, refactoring becomes difficult
Keep tests focused on public behavior
A mock-heavy London-style design can create tight coupling
terms: A failing test, pass it with minimal code, then clean up.
London: mocks, outside-in; Detroit (classicist): real objects, inside-out.

t4_1.desc: Testing pyramid, testing trophy, when to use unit vs integration vs E2E. The cost of each type. Avoiding the ice cream cone.
t4_1.what: Definition: Test types mix: static checks (TypeScript, ESLint), unit (pure logic), integration (components + hooks + network mock), E2E (real browser). Integration tests in the frontend often provide the best ROI.
t4_1.why: Unit tests are fast but give low confidence; E2E gives higher confidence but is slow/flaky. Maintaining the right cost-confidence balance is the testing architecture.
cons: Layer boundaries are a topic of debate within the team
gotchas: Don’t try to cover everything with E2E
Don’t make coverage percentage a goal
Quarantine flaky E2E tests; don’t ignore them
terms: Many unit, few integration, very few E2E.
Kent C. Dodds: static + unit + integration (most) + E2E.
Anti-pattern: too many E2E/manual, few unit — slow and flaky.
where: what and where testing will occur.

t4_2.what: Definition: GitHub Actions workflow: checkout → actions/setup-node with cache → install → lint/typecheck → unit tests → build → E2E (sharded). Required checks are set in branch protection, and the test report artifact is uploaded.
t4_2.why: Slow CI blocks developers and people start ignoring tests. Caching, parallel jobs, and fail-fast deliver feedback in minutes.
cons: CI cost and maintenance
gotchas: Keep the cache key based on the lockfile hash
Upload traces/reports artifacts on failure
Secrets are not available in PRs from forks
terms: Save install time by caching node_modules/Playwright browsers.
Run cheap checks (lint/typecheck) first, expensive ones later.

t4_3.what: Definition: A consumer test runs against a mock provider and creates a pact (JSON contract). In backend CI, the same pact is replayed against the real provider; a mismatch means a breaking change was caught before deployment.
t4_3.why: Even without E2E, it prevents bugs like “the backend renamed a field and the frontend broke”. It is most useful in microservices/multiple teams.
pros: Breaking API changes are caught early
gotchas: Specify only the parts of the contract that the consumer actually uses
You need to maintain provider states
It can be overkill for a small single-team app
terms: Frontend (consumer) specifies what it expects from the API.
Contract testing tool: the consumer test generates a pact file, which the provider verifies.
If the contract breaks, the provider build fails.

t4_4.what: Definition: Make performance part of the test suite: size-limit bundle budget, Lighthouse CI thresholds, and read LCP/CLS in Playwright using PerformanceObserver to assert.
t4_4.why: Performance regressions are silent; automated checks catch them at the PR stage, not after production.
cons: Lab numbers are noisy — keep a buffer on thresholds
gotchas: CI machines are variable — run multiple times / use relaxed thresholds
Complement with production RUM
Set realistic throttling
terms: Assert JS bundle size in CI.

t4_5.what: Definition: Common causes of flakiness: timing/race conditions, shared state, real network, random data, animation, test order dependence. Fix: auto-waiting/web-first assertions, isolated data, fake time, mocked network, and retry only for diagnosis.
t4_5.why: Flaky tests break trust — the team starts ignoring failures. Quarantine + tracking + root-cause fix should be a process.
cons: Root-cause hunting takes time
gotchas: Retries hide flakiness — track the rate
Don't depend on test order
Control real time/random/network
terms: Passes sometimes and fails sometimes without code changes.
Removing the flaky test from the main gate and tracking it separately.
Same input = same result: fixed time, seed, isolated data.
